newsitem.title: GERMANY: Berlin set to put Marlene Dietrich on the map.
newsitem.headline: Berlin set to put Marlene Dietrich on the map.

text.p: The legendary name of Marlene Dietrich looks set to take its place in the heart of Berlin despite resentment by some residents over her support for the Allied cause during World War Two.

After bickering in the Berlin district where the singer was born about whether to name a street or square after her, the city-centre Tiergarten district has stepped in with plans for its own Marlene Dietrich Square.

Horst Porath, Tiergarten's top planning official, said on Thursday Dietrich's name would be used for a new square being built as part of the Potsdamer Platz construction site, which will be home to a film museum and 3-D cinema.
"I thought this new location, which is also intended to have great cultural significance, would be a good and appropriate place for Marlene Dietrich," Porath told Reuters.

The seemingly innocuous idea of naming something after Dietrich, the star of "The Blue Angel", has proved contentious. Some Berliners see her as a traitor because she quit Germany, became an American citizen and entertained Allied troops during the war.
Porath said his plan had been agreed by all the local political parties and he was confident it would be approved by a full council meeting next month.

Councillors in the Schoeneberg district, where Dietrich was born in 1901, have long said they want to name a location after her but had failed to agree on a precise plan. Now Tiergarten appears to have stolen their thunder.
According to local planning rules, once one part of the city has used a street or square name, another cannot copy it.
"If they hadn't argued so much in Schoeneberg, then this wouldn't have been possible," Porath said.
Dietrich, who is buried in Berlin, arrived in Hollywood in 1930 and took up U.S. citizenship in 1939 at the height of her career. A recluse in her later years, she died in Paris in 1992.

The Potsdamer Platz area used to be one the livliest parts of Berlin, a crossroads between East and West because of a nearby major rail station, but was destroyed by Allied bombing and lay derelict in the no man's land around the Berlin Wall.

Other likely candidates for a street name in the area include the late Herbert von Karajan, acclaimed conductor of the Berlin Philharmonic, the fairy-tale-telling Brothers Grimm and General Ludwig Beck, a wartime army officer who opposed Hitler.
The new quarter is planned as a glittering mix of high-class hotels, banks, company headquarters and a German Film Museum, which will also house a collection of Dietrich memorabilia.
